1:
The opening verse is felt to be misplaced. Gill says it belongs more properly to the preceding chapter, which it should have concluded, and denies they are the words of the prophet, taking them for the angel telling him what he had done at the very beginning of that monarchy, when the Mede became king of Babylon; he notes that the Septuagint and Arabic versions read the first year of Cyrus, which was the same time, since the two reigned together. Ellicott likewise connects the words closely with the last verse of the chapter before, and takes the allusion most probably to the fall of Babylon and the return from the Exile, when, as at the Exodus, the angel of the Lord went before his people. Henry hears the angel letting the prophet know the good service he has done the nation, standing as a strength and fortress to the king who destroyed Babylon and confirming him in his resolution to release the captives.

Calvin sets out the alternatives and takes a third course. Some think the angel fought for the Persian king, having defended that monarchy from the beginning; others refer the words to Michael, which Calvin calls forced and cold. He reads the argument as one from the greater to the less, citing a line of Ovid to the effect that one who has been able to preserve may surely destroy. So the angel says that he erected the monarchy, was the servant of God in transferring rule from the Medes and Chaldeans to the Persians, and set Darius upon the throne, and therefore has him wholly in his power. In speaking so, Calvin adds, the angel claims nothing for himself but speaks in the person of God, since angels have no power distinct from his.

The three kings and the fourth are counted almost alike. Clarke names them after the reigning king as his son, then the impostor who pretended to be another son, then the son of Hystaspes; the fourth is Xerxes, of whom Justin said that though rivers were dried up by his armies his wealth remained unexhausted, and whose forces Herodotus, who lived in that time, numbered in millions. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same four, reasoning that since the prophecy originates in the third year of the reigning king the three who shall yet arise are his three successors, and that all said of the fourth agrees perfectly with the last of them. Ellicott says it is hard to say who they were but reaches the same result, observing that those four were selected whose influence was most prominent in its bearings upon Israel, and that the reckoning dates from the reigning king, the short reign of the impostor not being counted. Wesley notes that there were more kings of Persia, but that they had no concern with the people of God.

What the chapter is about divides those who say. Clarke lays out a scheme running from the partition of the empire of Alexander through the two kingdoms north and south of Judea, then to the Romans, then to the Church under that power, then to Antichrist, and at last to the powers that push at him in the latter days, taking the king of the south there for the dominion of the Arabs. Ellicott warns that from this point the difficulties are almost insuperable. It has been customary from the time of Jerome to explain most of what follows of the Greek houses that divided the empire, but he questions whether that interpretation is correct and whether the revelation does not still await fulfilment: mere similarity between what is predicted here and what occurred then is not sufficient to limit the prophecy to those times, and since history repeats itself, the events which preceded that persecutor may be typical of what will occur before the coming of the Messiah.
3:
The mighty king is identified by everyone but one. Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Calvin all name Alexander, Gill noting that he rose a hundred years after the expedition of Xerxes and, as Jerome says, conquered the Illyrians, Thracians, Greece and Thebes, passed into Asia, put the generals of Darius to flight, and took Sardis. Keil and Delitzsch treat the Macedonian kingdom as given only in brief notices, calling its founder a hero-king whose ruling according to his own will marks a power irresistible and boundless, and quote Curtius, that though he owed much to his valour he owed more to a fortune which he alone of mortals held in his power. Ellicott refuses the identification. No clue is given to show over what nation this king reigns; by the context he might be a Greek or a Persian, or belong to a kingdom not yet mentioned. He grants that the self-will spoken of was characteristic of Alexander, but holds there is nothing in the context making it necessary to limit the passage to him, and that some autocrat may arise in the latter times to whom it will apply with greater force.

The breaking of the kingdom is read for its suddenness. Keil and Delitzsch note that the particle states the rising of the king and the destruction of his kingdom as synchronous, expressing with great force how short its duration was; Ellicott says the same, that the moment he has arisen he will come to nothing. Calvin describes the end: he had arrived at his height, fell suddenly sick, and died at Babylon. Historians, viewing him as a remarkable example of singular valour, have supposed he was poisoned by treachery, but Calvin thinks his own intemperate drinking was the poison, since he was seized with disease amidst his cups. He adds that the power was not so much extinguished as broken into separate parts, the chiefs who were his generals drawing the spoils to themselves as if torn from the body of their master.

On the exclusion of his posterity Clarke gives the roll of murders: a wife killed by the other wife, a brother and his queen killed by order of the mother of the king, that mother killed by the soldiers in revenge, a son and his mother slain by order of one general, and later another son and his mother murdered by another, so that within fifteen years not one of the family remained alive. Blood calls for blood, Clarke writes, and a retributive providence destroyed all the posterity of the great butcher of men. Wesley notes that the successors did not reign as kings at first but only as captains, all four falling short of what he had ruled. Ellicott again allows the explanation but not the certainty, holding the language too indefinite to make such an identification sure.

The two kingdoms are then set. Gill takes the king of the south for Egypt, which lay south of Syria, and names the general who had Egypt for his share. Henry sets out both houses, the one in Egypt and the one in Syria, and observes that both were strong against Judah, the southern king having taken Jerusalem on a sabbath under pretence of a friendly visit. Calvin differs on the grammar. Many take the clause in one context, but he thinks the angel transfers the discourse to the northern king, the conjunction being taken in the sense of opposing, so that one of the princes of Alexander grows strong against the other; and he observes that the northern kingdom was much larger and wealthier, especially when Asia Minor was added to it. Ellicott finds the phrase equally obscure, notes that both Greek versions make one of the princes of the southern king stronger than his former master, and asks how the founder of the northern house could be called a prince of the southern king.
6:
The alliance and the marriage are told at length by four voices and doubted by one. Gill names the two kings, the second of the southern house, who gathered the great library and had the law of Moses translated into Greek, and the third of the northern, whose surname the Milesians gave him for delivering them from a tyrant; weary of war, they entered into confederacy about seventy years after the death of Alexander. Clarke supplies the terms and the sequel: Berenice was married to Antiochus Theos on condition that he put away his former wife Laodice and her children, which he did; but he recalled them, and Laodice, fearing that Berenice might be recalled in turn, had him poisoned and her murdered, and set her own son upon the throne. Wesley adds that she was brought to Pelusium with an infinite sum of gold and silver for her dowry. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the grammar, taking the word rendered agreement as rectitude, designating the relation between the two rulers.

Ellicott finds the whole identification unsatisfactory. If the joining together refers to that marriage and the agreement to its terms, then history is irreconcilable with the prophecy; it does not appear that the marriage affected the Jewish people more than any other, though the revelation was said to bear upon their future; and more than fifty years intervene between the events supposed to be meant. He refers the language instead to what is named elsewhere as a characteristic of the last empire, attempts to consolidate earthly powers by political marriages, which do not mark that era more than the times of Ahab. On the clause about retaining, he takes the meaning to be that the marriage will not accomplish its intended purpose, the southern king becoming not more independent of his rival but more subjected to him, which he observes did not happen with the two kings usually named.

The avenger from her roots is agreed to be her brother. Keil and Delitzsch make the roots her parents and the offspring a brother rather than a descendant, and note that the figure recalls a verse of Isaiah. Clarke recounts the campaign, in which he took all Asia from Mount Taurus to India and returned with forty thousand talents of silver and two thousand five hundred images, without the northern king daring to offer him battle; he apologises for touching these facts so lightly, for fear of extending his notes to an immoderate length. Calvin adds that the fortified cities surrendered from terror, and that the northern king, suspecting his younger brother, thought it safest to treat with his enemy. Ellicott again withholds assent: the coincidence between history and prophecy is far from establishing the explanation, and commentators do not agree even on what the roots mean.

The carrying away of the gods is explained as custom and as policy. Keil and Delitzsch call it a usual custom with conquerors, and note that in the images the gods themselves were carried away, so that they are called their gods. Gill reports from Jerom that among the images were many carried out of Egypt by a former conqueror, and that replacing them in their proper temples gained the king the affection of a people much addicted to idolatry, whence his surname of benefactor. Calvin says the event proved the prophecy true, and that the interposed particle amplifies the subject, showing how unequal the peace was. On the last clause Clarke and Wesley count the years, the northern king dying an exile by a fall from his horse; Ellicott, reading the preposition differently, takes it that the southern king shall stand as an ally of the northern for several years, or else abstain from him, and remarks that nothing here lets us infer what history states, that the northern king was crippled by a defeat and his fleet dispersed by a storm.
9:
The return of the southern king is read two ways. Gill takes him as coming into his own kingdom, or else into the kingdom he had conquered; Clarke explains the return by a sedition at home which obliged him to hurry back, else he had wholly destroyed the northern kingdom, and Wesley adds that he went home with a booty of forty thousand talents of silver. Calvin joins the clause to the verse before, reading the coming and returning emphatically as a march free of all harass, fear and danger. Ellicott inverts the sense on grammatical grounds: by the Hebrew the words stand in the genitive, so that the northern king comes into the kingdom of the southern and returns to his own land, apparently without gaining any advantage.

Whose sons are stirred up turns on a single pronoun. Keil and Delitzsch refer the suffix to the northern king, and say all interpreters do so but one, whose reading they judge shattered by the contents of the next verse, since the rage of the southern king supposes that the other had provoked it by an assault. Ellicott notes the same divergence, that the pronoun refers by the Hebrew to the northern king though the Greek and the English make it his rival, and that a marginal alternative reads son rather than sons. Gill, Clarke and Calvin all name the two brothers, the elder dying early, poisoned by two of his own generals when he could not pay the multitude he had raised, so that only one of them came and overflowed and passed through.

The battle at the frontier is described with confidence by three and with hesitation by one. Clarke names the place, gives the northern army as sixty-two thousand foot, six thousand horse and a hundred and two elephants, and has the southern king gain a complete victory, the neighbouring towns declaring for the victor and the beaten king retreating to Antioch to solicit peace. Calvin gives different figures and explains why the brothers thought the moment ripe: the southern king was hated and despised by his own people, having put to death his father, his mother and his brother, so that the title meaning lover of his father was applied to him by way of ridicule and as a mark of disgrace. Gill says he was ironically named for the same reason, and was naturally sluggish though provoked at last. Ellicott says the ambiguity of the verse is very great, since the pronoun may refer to either king, and that only the added words naming the northern king make the first of the two interpretations most probable.

What the victor did with his victory is agreed. Ellicott finds the next verse ambiguous too, uncertain whether the multitude or the king is its subject and whether the verb is active or passive, and offers two renderings; but he takes the last clause to mean that the victor did not prove so successful as he had hoped, being content to regain the towns taken from him instead of striking a decisive blow. Clarke says he might have dispossessed his rival of the whole empire had he improved his victory, but gave way to pride and a criminally sensual life and made peace on dishonourable terms, so that his subjects were displeased and his kingdom not strengthened. Calvin adds the sequel at home, the murder of his wife and the surrender of the government to a favourite, and names the cause of the fall as idleness and drunkenness and a care for nothing but banquets, after he had been raised to the clouds by his victories. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the correlation of the clauses: as the multitude rises up, so his heart is lifted up.
13:
The return of the northern king is dated by the death of his rival. Gill has him take advantage of the minority of a child of five, entering into a league with the king of Macedon to divide the southern kingdom between them, and marching into the disputed provinces; Clarke reckons about fourteen years, with a much larger army and riches collected in an eastern expedition. Keil and Delitzsch note the phrase about the end of times, taking the word for times as stretching over years, and observe that with the article these are in prophetic discourse the times determined by God. Calvin adds what the others omit, that the southern court sent an embassy to Rome, and that the Senate, eager to be involved in all the business of the world, commanded the northern king to desist from the war.

Ellicott turns the same verse into an objection. On the hypothesis that these chapters refer to that period, he says, it is surprising that nothing is said of the religious persecutions the Jews in Egypt suffered under the southern king, who after his victory attempted to enter the Holy Place. They suffered considerably from both parties throughout the whole period; yet though the prophecy is supposed to have been written for their comfort at that very juncture, not a word bears allusion to them.

The robbers of the people are the crux. Clarke takes them for Jews who revolted from their religion and joined the southern party, and explains the phrase about establishing the vision as their hope of building a temple in Egypt like the one at Jerusalem, thinking thereby to fulfil a prediction that the two peoples should be one. Calvin derives the word from a root meaning to break or dissipate and takes it of factious men, since the people had no chance of standing except by remaining quiet and united; he reports the interpreters who apply it to the younger Onias, who seized Heliopolis and built a temple there, pleading a prophecy of Isaiah on his side, and answers that the prophecy foretold rather the spread of true worship. Ellicott says the words can only refer to Jews who committed violent breaches of the Law, and finds the significant part of the verse in their falling, which seems to mean that their conduct brought them just the reverse of what they had expected. Keil and Delitzsch note that almost all interpreters since Jerome refer the clause to the later oppression, and allow it so far as the apostasy of one party helped to bring that oppression about.

The campaign that follows is agreed, and its effect on the land disputed. Gill and Clarke both narrate the defeat of the southern general at the springs of Jordan and his flight to Sidon, where famine forced him to surrender; Gill adds from Josephus that the people voluntarily submitted and received the conqueror into their city. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for fortified city stands without the article and so collectively, and that the jussive forms in the verses following show these undertakings to be carried on under a divine decree. Calvin dwells on the epithet given to the land, which was excellent by no natural advantage but because God had chosen it for his dwelling-place, and observes that the Church on its pilgrimage enjoys no freedom from affliction, since it is profitable for the sons of God to be humbled under the cross. Clarke and Wesley both read the last clause favourably, Clarke rendering it that the land shall be perfected in his hand, since the conqueror showed the people great favour, bringing back the dispersed and freeing the priests from tribute. Ellicott objects that history does not speak of any acts of destruction committed by him there, and renders the phrase literally as destruction being in his hand.
17:
The marriage is read as a stratagem. Clarke has the northern king prefer fraud to force, proposing his daughter, called the daughter of women for her great beauty, and appearing to act with none but upright views while intending her as a snare; but the interests of her husband became dearer to her, and by her means he was put on his guard. Calvin says she preserved her conjugal fidelity and never listened to the cunning designs of her father. On the phrase about upright ones the voices divide: Clarke takes it of the manner, that he would make all things straight; Wesley and others whom Calvin reports take it of the Jews who openly espoused his cause, so called as a mark of honour; Calvin thinks that too forced. Ellicott renders the words literally as all that is right and allows that persons may be meant. Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that makes the king come against the strength of the whole kingdom, since the noun means strength as a property, not power over something.

The turn to the isles is explained geographically. Gill and Calvin both note the Jewish custom of calling maritime places islands, Calvin extending the term to Asia Minor, Greece, Cyprus and the islands of the Mediterranean, as the people were not well skilled in navigation. Keil and Delitzsch resist an emendation, since in turning from Egypt to the islands the king turns his face back toward his own land. On the prince who ends the reproach, Clarke names a consul who beat him at a mountain pass and expelled him from Greece, imposing fifteen thousand talents by instalments without losing a battle or taking a false step. Ellicott doubts even the case of the noun, since one tradition takes it as accusative, so that the king causes to cease the princes who were his reproach and they return it upon him.

The retreat and the death are told with wide variation. Gill has him flee to two cities and then to his capital, the fort of his land. Clarke says that, unable to raise the money, he marched east to exact arrears and, attempting to plunder a temple, was killed by the populace; but he lists three other accounts, concludes that the manner of his death is uncertain, and suggests that this very circumstance may be what is meant by the words that he shall not be found. Calvin offers the same two possibilities, the tumult at the temple or the outcome of the war.

The raiser of taxes is identified alike and glossed differently. Gill rejects three other candidates and names the eldest son, obliged to raise a thousand talents yearly for twelve years, so that taxing took up his reign. Clarke adds that he sent his treasurer to seize the money in the temple and was destroyed neither in anger nor in battle but basely, by that treasurer, who hoped to reign in his stead; Wesley says by poison. Calvin reports a reading that would praise him for lessening the imposts of his father, but says historians show it false and condemn his rapacity, since luxury and prodigality always draw cruelty in exaction after them. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both widen the word: it denotes not a collector of tribute but a taskmaster who urges on the people and oppresses them as cattle, and the glory of the kingdom means its richest parts, not necessarily the holy land. Ellicott closes the first part of the prophecy here, observing that its notes of time are very scanty and that nothing implies any change of sovereigns except at two verses, so that in their natural sense these verses speak of only two southern kings and one northern, the whole being eschatological and referring to two powers which will affect the destiny of the people of God in the last times.
21:
The vile person is identified by all but one and characterised at length. Gill takes the word to signify despicable, and lists what earned the name: a mean and ignoble life at Rome as a hostage for eleven or twelve years, while the other hostages were changed at three years end, and a course of behaviour that made him ridiculous, rambling the streets with a servant or two, conversing with tradesmen about their trades, drinking with strangers and people of low life, throwing his money among the rabble and stones at those who followed him, and washing at the public baths among the common people. Clarke quotes Polybius to the same effect, that he resorted to the common shops and prattled with the workmen, frequented the taverns and ate and drank with the meanest fellows, singing debauched songs; whence a contemporary writer turned his surname of the Illustrious into a nickname meaning the Madman. Calvin reports the same nickname and adds that he was a monster puffed up with various vices, of a slavish and flattering temperament while afraid, and beyond all bounds in cruelty when he was not. Henry says the heathen writers describe him as rude and boisterous, base and sordid, with such unaccountable whims that some took him to be silly and others mad, so that his character was the reverse of his surname.

Why the honour was not given him is variously supplied. Clarke has him at Athens on his way from Rome when his father died, with the treasurer and several others already claiming the throne; he came in peaceably and obtained the kingdom by flatteries, flattering two neighbouring kings for their help, the Romans with an embassy and the arrears of tribute, and his own people, who flattered him back with the title of the Illustrious. Wesley says neither peers nor people gave it him, and that he was not the heir but the nephew, and crept in by flatteries. Calvin offers a second reason he thinks equally probable, that his predecessor left a successor whose rights this perfidious plotter set aside, so that he acquired the kingdom fraudulently.

Ellicott alone withholds the identification, and does so carefully. The moral character of the man is what is especially described, he says, and the words following explain that he was not worthy of receiving royal majesty. The description certainly agrees very closely with the persecutor generally named, just as his predecessors resembled at various points the kings spoken of in the earlier verses; and Ellicott quotes Jerome to the effect that early interpreters, finding much that suited that persecutor, held him a type of the antichrist, so that what was partly accomplished in him would be wholly accomplished in the other. But on the last clause Ellicott dissents outright: the king is represented as taking possession by craft, unexpectedly, and gaining his end by intrigues and hypocritical conduct, and it does not appear that this was done by the man usually named.

Henry and Keil and Delitzsch set the passage in a larger frame. Henry observes that the troubles under the earlier kings were not foretold so particularly, because the people then had living prophets to encourage them, whereas these were foretold because prophecy would cease before them and they would find it necessary to have recourse to the written word; and he notes that as the prophets, foretelling the prosperity of the church, slide insensibly into the kingdom of Christ, so in foretelling its troubles they use expressions reaching further, to the rise and ruin of the antichrist. Keil and Delitzsch divide the description into two stages, the first running through the gradual rise to power, the war for supremacy, the rising against the covenant people and the desecration of the sanctuary, and the effect of all this upon the people of God.
22:
The flood of arms is read of the rival claimants or of the invading armies. Gill takes the forces of two neighbouring kings as the inundation that bore down the party of the usurper, or else the Egyptian armies which had used to overrun the provinces and were now overwhelmed themselves. Clarke says the arms overflown were his competitors for the crown, dissipated by his arrival from Athens, which disconcerted their measures. Calvin sets the scene more fully: a portion of the court favoured the lawful heir, the counsels of Egypt secretly supplied that faction, and all pitied the lot of the ward, so that the new king had much trouble with his own people and with neighbouring nations. The metaphor of a deluge marks not only the victory but its great facility, and Calvin adds that this king was in truth the scourge of God. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the phrase as armies overflowing the land, swept away before him by yet stronger military forces.

The prince of the covenant is the disputed phrase. Clarke and Wesley both make him the high priest, removed to make way for a brother who had given a great sum, and then for a worse man who offered more. Keil and Delitzsch reject the identification: the expression is analogous to phrases meaning men of a covenant, and the absence of the article shows it is to be taken generally, while the murder in question does not relate to the matter before us and is not warranted by the facts of history. Ellicott agrees, taking the words in contrast with the hostile armies of the first clause, so that they mean those who were at peace with him, the noun being collective; there is no reason, he says, for supposing that the high priest was ever called by such a title.

The league and the deceit are then explained. Gill offers two candidates for the confederate, a nephew or the southern king with whom a league was made while the sister of the northern king lived. Calvin gives the same and explains the pause in the fighting: the country was impoverished by continual war, so a temporary peace was negotiated, the surviving sister making an honourable excuse; but the uncle attacked suddenly with a small force, and the boy, expecting a lasting friendship, lost some of his cities. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase to mean that from the time when he made the covenant with them he practised deceit; Ellicott says the same, that from the time he first becomes their confederate he works deceitfully, coming up with hostile intent accompanied only by a few people, and so throwing off their guard those he would destroy.

The entering upon the fattest places is agreed to be strategy dressed as generosity. Clarke gives the detail: he became profuse in his liberalities, scattering the spoil of temples and the riches of his friends as well as his own revenues, and sometimes going into the streets to throw about a handful of money, crying that whoever fortune sent it to might take it. Wesley says it obliged his confidants the faster to him. Calvin reports two readings of the clause, one making the scattering a distribution among his soldiers to conciliate them, the other a spoiling like a robber, and prefers the second; he notes that the plans against the strongholds were deferred to a more suitable time. Ellicott gives the same two options and prefers the first, as more in accordance with the deceit the prophecy attributes to the king; he takes the time named as the end of the time decreed by God. On the war that follows, Clarke and Wesley both attribute the defeat of the southern king to the corruption of his own ministers, and Calvin agrees that he had courage enough to resist had he not been betrayed by his adherents.
26:
The treachery at the table is agreed. Gill and Clarke both make the destroyers the courtiers and generals in the confidence and pay of the southern king, corrupted by his rival. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the phrase as his table-companions, and note that the first clause points to treachery by which the battle was lost and the war made fruitless; they reject a rendering that would make the army rush away in flight, since the verb cannot bear it. Ellicott says the context points to treachery, though he observes that history is silent about any such betrayal of the king he thinks meant. Calvin sets the leaders against the common soldiers, who discharged their duty without sparing life or blood, and draws a lesson on the ordinary situation of kings: they choose counsellors not by honesty but by congeniality of tastes, so that an avaricious or cruel king surrounds himself with men who will check none of it, and deserves the treachery he gets.

The two liars at one table are counted differently. Keil and Delitzsch insist there are only two kings here, the north and the south already named, and that a third is introduced from history rather than found in the text; they call the various pairings arbitrary, and cite Jerome that the two fraudulent hearts cannot be demonstrated from history. Ellicott likewise holds the context opposed to any reference to a combination of two kings against a third, and takes the object of the paragraph to be that the southern king was trying to fight his rival with his own weapon of deceit, and that the plots of each fail. Clarke fills in what the lies were on either side. Calvin adds why such detail is given: had the angel said only that there would be war and then a peace, it would not have sustained the pious, but when the particulars are so exactly foretold the faithful have no reason to doubt that God has spoken. Wesley and Ellicott both take the appointed time as the time fixed by God, which no man can hasten.

The turn against the holy covenant is where the chapter changes character. Gill and Clarke both narrate the return with spoil, Clarke adding the report of the death of the king that had provoked rejoicing at Jerusalem, the deposed high priest raising forces on the strength of it, and the storming of the city that followed, with forty thousand slain and as many sold. Keil and Delitzsch insist that the holy covenant means not the covenant people but the divine institution itself, and quote Calvin with approval that the simpler sense is that he wages war against God. Calvin himself gives that reading and calls the other too cold and forced, adding that the king would willingly have stripped the whole temple but that God restrained him.

The last expedition fails, and the voices agree why. Gill dates it by the setting up of a brother as king at Alexandria, and says the pretext of restoring the deposed king covered a design to seize the kingdom. Clarke says he threw off the mask when the two brothers united their counsel and strength, and marched by easy stages to the capital, but had neither the success of the first campaign nor of the second; Wesley says the same in a line. Calvin names the cause plainly, that the siege was raised when the Roman envoy arrived. Keil and Delitzsch explain the ships that come against him, the name standing for Cyprus and so for vessels coming from the west, from the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean; they note that one tradition read it of a Macedonian fleet, and that what is historically verified is that a Roman embassy appeared with a fleet and imperiously commanded the king to desist from his undertaking and return to his own land.
30:
The ships from the west are identified without much dispute. Gill names the three envoys sent in ships from Macedonia to require the king to desist and quit Egypt, and notes that Macedonia is so called in the Maccabees. Calvin surveys the word across Scripture and concludes it covers the Macedonians, Greeks and Italians, adding that here the case is free from doubt, since it was the Romans and not the Greeks who restrained him. Ellicott notes that the Greek version explains it of the Romans, and that one translator apparently imagined the islanders came as allies to the king rather than against him.

The scene at the circle is told by two. Clarke reports that the envoy handed over the letters of the senate commanding an end to the war, and when the king said he would consult his friends, drew a circle round him in the sand with his staff and forbade him to pass it until he had given a definitive answer; the king, intimidated, promised obedience and marched home within days. Calvin adds that the two had been acquainted when the king was a hostage at Rome, that he received the envoy graciously and even wished to salute him, his disposition being naturally servile, and that the envoy rejected all these advances and told him to keep his familiarities for private intercourse. Ellicott gives the phrase about grieving its literal sense, that he shall lose heart, and quotes the historian who says he was stupefied by so violent a command.

What he did on his return is described by all. Clarke names the general sent with twenty-two thousand men, the plundering and burning of the city, the castle built on an eminence commanding the temple, and the decree that all should conform to Grecian worship. Wesley says his heart boiled with rancour, and names the two apostates who solicited him. Ellicott identifies those who forsook the covenant as men anxious to make all their institutions Greek, abandoning its outward sign and taking Greek names. Calvin refuses to read the arms of the next verse as the garrison imposed on the city, calling that far-fetched, and takes them of the apostates and forsakers of the Law: the king should not contend in his own strength but rely on the assistance of a party at Jerusalem which willingly prostituted itself to his will.

On that verse Clarke breaks with everyone. After this king, he says, arms means the Romans, since arms in this prophecy everywhere denote military power and standing up denotes that power in activity and conquering; following Newton he holds that the prophet, having described the kings of the north and south down to the conquest of Macedon, leaves off the Greeks and begins on the Romans, and that the polluting of the sanctuary came long after, when a temple to a heathen god was built where the temple of God had stood. Gill names the generals who held the land for the king. Ellicott takes the arms for military assistance, contrasted in the next verse with the help given by the apostates, and reads the sanctuary of strength as two nouns in apposition naming the temple, which was the spiritual support of the people as well as a powerful fortress. Calvin explains the same epithet as an assurance to the pious that God had not given way to the tyrant, his authority standing untouched though his temple was polluted; and observes that the king might have overthrown the whole Law in a moment but chose first to mingle many superstitions with it, to estrange the people by degrees. Henry says the remainder of the prophecy is very difficult and that commentators differ much, but that the account seems to pass from this king to the antichrist. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the arms stand up by his command.
32:
The corrupting of the wicked is explained by what they had already become. Gill takes them for those who forsook the law and violated the covenant of circumcision, and says the king corrupted them by good words and fair speeches, by gifts and presents, until they became his instruments to seduce others. Ellicott traces the progress: these persons had begun with indifference to true religion and are now intolerant of it, and the word rendered corrupt means literally to make profane, so that they have become as the heathen. Keil and Delitzsch spend their space rejecting three renderings of the first phrase, that it means those who sinfully make a covenant, or sinners among the covenant people, or those who condemn the covenant by rejecting circumcision; the last they call altogether arbitrary. Calvin makes the apostates the arms of the king, since he would not have dared to offer such insults to the temple without their help, and observes that ambition and avarice alone had impelled them to unite with a tyrant who was the avowed enemy of their religion.

The people who know their God are read as a remnant. Ellicott says that while the large mass becomes obedient to the persecutor, a party of true believers remains who confirm the covenant and succeed in their attempt; and he adds that in all times of persecution there will be such a remnant, though it may be very small. Keil and Delitzsch make the same contrast the point of the verse, the ungodly wholly apostatising while the pious are strengthened in their confidence. Clarke reads it all of another age, taking the wicked for those pressed by the Roman power to sacrifice to the statues of the emperors, and the strong for genuine Christians strengthened by grace, who continued steadfast in all temptations and enjoyed a good conscience.

Who the understanding are divides the readings again. Keil and Delitzsch insist the word does not mean teachers but those who have insight, that is, the pious just named, since in the older usage wisdom and the fear of God are correlative ideas; and they note that the many with the article are the great multitude moved by the judicious behaviour of the pious to hold fast the law. Ellicott agrees that their example is the instruction, showing the rest whither they are drifting. Calvin insists on the grammar in the other direction: some take the first word transitively, as those who shall instruct, which is wrong, and they show their ignorance by supposing a relative understood before the next verb; the simple sense is that those who are wise among the people shall teach many. Gill takes them for men of better understanding whom God raises up in the worst times of apostasy, who strengthened the weak and established the wavering, and names two such from the histories. Calvin thinks the priests are chiefly meant, the greater part having failed and implicated the foolish vulgar in their wickedness, but does not restrict the wise to them, since others laboured to recall the wandering into the way of salvation.

The suffering is left general. Keil and Delitzsch note that those who fall are not the multitude but a number of the understanding, and that the effect of their falling is felt by the whole people. Ellicott says the prophecy obviously refers to martyrdom, though whether to the sufferings of those who understand or of those instructed is not clear, and probably both are intended; he takes the deaths recorded in the histories as typical of the sufferings of the Church in the last times. Clarke keeps to his own scheme, referring the sword and flame and captivity and spoil to persecutions endured with little intermission for three hundred years.
34:
The little help is identified alike by three and differently by two. Gill names the priest of Modin and his five sons, and notes that even a hostile ancient critic interpreted the verse of him; the help was little, he says, because they were persons of small figure who began with a handful of men, could not restore the land to its former liberty, and whose help did not last long before the enemy returned. Calvin agrees and asks what they could do to resist so powerful a king, Judea being nothing beside the northern kingdom, especially since the people had destroyed their own power by violating treaties and corrupting the majority of themselves, so that there was neither skill nor plan nor concert among them. Ellicott says the help will be small either compared with their present needs or with the great help to come when the tribulation attains its greatest severity, and observes that it prevented the faithful from disappearing entirely. Keil and Delitzsch reject the suggestion that the word is spoken contemptuously, and insist it is called little only by comparison with the complete destruction of the oppressor at the time of the end; the little help consisted in this, that by the rising up of those who understood, the destruction of the worship of God was prevented.

Gill and Clarke both report a different scheme. Gill notes that one interpreter, and Newton with him, understood the help of the relief given the Christians under two emperors. Clarke adopts that reading outright, taking the fall as the last and longest persecution, the little help as the emperor who ended persecution and promoted the temporal prosperity of the Christian Church while adding little to its spiritual strength, and the many who cleave with flatteries as those who became Christians because the emperor was one.

The flatterers are the shadow on the deliverance. Ellicott says dissimulation will cause some to declare themselves upon the side of those who understand, and notes it as a feature of religious persecutions generally, that as one party gains in power and its prospects brighten it gains fresh adherents. Calvin puts it more bitterly: even from this small number the angel cuts off the greater part, so that of the few who dared oppose the madness of the tyrant many were hypocrites. He adds that though the chapter must be interpreted of that king, the teaching is equally for later readers, since the same old enemy assails the Church partly from without and partly from within.

Why the understanding are allowed to fall is answered in three stages. Ellicott lays them out: to try, that is, to refine as a precious metal is refined by fire; to purge, that is, to separate the bad from the good; and to make white, that is, to cause them to become completely purified. In this way the dissemblers are made known, the patient example of the sufferers being followed by the faithful while the flatterers become open apostates. Keil and Delitzsch say the church has needed this purifying process of affliction in all periods of its history, that the falling means not only death in battle but imprisonment and plunder, and that the pronoun refers to the whole company of the people of God rather than to any one class among them. Gill insists the falling is not into sin, nor from the religion they profess, but into distresses and calamities for a steadfast adherence to the worship of God. Calvin says the phrase implies the perishing of the very flower of the Church, since the greater part of a people flies off when religion requires the sacrifice of life, and calls those intelligent who, forgetful of their own lives, offer themselves in sacrifice to God, incurring universal hatred and prepared to meet death with fortitude.
36:
Here the identification breaks down, and every voice says so. Gill denies the verse can be applied to the king hitherto described, since he could not do as he would, being curbed by the Romans, and many things that follow do not suit him. Keil and Delitzsch make the objection in detail: to raise oneself above every god means above the gods of the heathen as well as the God of Israel, and this does not agree with that king, who was no atheist, wished rather to render the worship of one Greek god universal, and whose spoiling of a temple does not amount to raising himself above every god. Ellicott says the features of the earlier king are gradually fading from the portrait and that his main object was to force the Greek gods upon the people, so that the character described here finds its parallel rather in what Paul says of the antichrist. Calvin, after surveying the opinions, sets aside the reading that makes this king the type and another the antitype, probable though he calls it, on the ground that he did not long survive the pollution of the temple and that what follows by no means suits the occurrences of that time.

Where they go instead is where they divide. Gill and Clarke both look to a later ecclesiastical power, Clarke observing that in the language of this prophecy a king stands for a power or a kingdom, and that such a power did arise, acting arbitrarily against all laws human and divine. Calvin reports that some refer the prophecy to two later figures, and that the clause about the desire of women is what gives that view its probability. Wesley takes the opposite course, holding that the words principally refer to the earlier king and had their primary accomplishment in him, though he was an eminent type to whom much that follows may be applied by way of accommodation.

The clause about the God of his fathers is read of a discarded inheritance. Keil and Delitzsch take it as casting aside the worship transmitted to him from his fathers, and again say this does not accord with the earlier king; they quote a scholar who doubts the decree usually cited in evidence, since no profane historian records it, nor Josephus, nor the second book of the Maccabees in the parallel passages. Ellicott notes on the other side that Polybius says the king exceeded all kings in the sacrifices he offered and the honours he paid the gods. Calvin says plainly that those who explain the prophecy of him have trouble with these words, since he neither neglected all deities nor the god of his fathers.

The desire of women is the most contested phrase in the chapter. Ellicott sets out the alternatives: language elsewhere about delectable things has led some to think an idol is meant, and a particular goddess has been named, but the context leads rather to human affection, or something else highly prized by women, since the clause about regarding no god would be unmeaning if a god were designated here. Clarke reads it of the discouraging and proscribing of marriage under pretence of greater chastity. Calvin reports the two readings current in his day, one turning on a licence given to many wives, which he says destroys conjugal love, since where rivalry exists between wives there can be no happiness, and one turning on an enforced celibacy by which the honour of marriage is trodden under foot. On the last clause Ellicott adds his own suggestion, that the god this king honours in place of the one he has rejected is no proper name at all but simply fortresses, so that his whole religion is the taking of them: war is everything to him, and to war, as if it were a god, he does honour with all his wealth.
38:
The god of forces sets the interpreters hunting. Keil and Delitzsch report that the word is now generally acknowledged not to be the proper name of a god, though several older versions took it so, and then list the candidates: the god of war, the chief god of the capitol to whom the king meant to build a temple at Antioch, the same god under another title, and, by an emendation of the text, a Phoenician deity. They dismiss them all by the following clause, since none of these could be called a god unknown to his fathers. Wesley names one of the same candidates without hesitation, saying it was never introduced among the northern people until this king did it. Ellicott, having already denied that the word is a name at all, needs no candidate.

Calvin takes the apparent contradiction as the key. At first glance the statements seem opposed, that this king should despise all deities and yet worship one in no ordinary way; and this, he says, agrees very well with the Romans if their dispositions and manners be studied. They treated the worship of their deities simply as a matter of business, and so were destitute of any perception of the divinity while remaining pretenders to religion; other profane nations groped in darkness, but these were subject neither to error nor ignorance, and manifested a gross contempt of God while maintaining the appearance of piety. They fetched deities from every quarter of the world and worshipped them in common with other nations, yet treated all other rites as worthless; and their supreme god was supreme only under the additional title that bound him to themselves, since without it he was nobody at all.

Gill and Clarke read the honouring of the god as a later cult of protectors. Gill notes that the word signifies towers, strong holds and fortresses, and that the earliest advocates of the practice used those very titles of the departed whom they invoked as guardians. Clarke gives the marginal rendering as gods protectors, and understands the worship of guardians and mediators to the neglect of the true God and the one Mediator; he observes that such figures were utterly unknown as invocable guardians in the primitive apostolic Church, dates the beginning of the practice to the fourth century and its establishment to a general council, and applies the gold and silver and precious stones to the shrines, images and costly apparel of a later age.

The last verse is read either of a religion or of a policy. Keil and Delitzsch give the sense as a whole: with the help of this god unknown to his fathers he proceeds against the strong fortresses, rewarding with honour, might and wealth those who acknowledge him. They complain that most modern interpreters separate the two halves of the verse, and reject in turn a supplied demonstrative, the interpretation of the armed fortresses as temples, and an emendation that would have him prepare a people of a strange god for those fortresses. Ellicott agrees that all who acknowledge him are rewarded, and takes the dividing of the land as a reward offered to those who join his ranks, noting that no such conduct is recorded of the earlier king, though bribery was not an unusual mode of persuasion with him. Clarke prefers a rendering that makes the defenders of the strongholds the objects: they shall be multiplied in honour, made to rule over many, and the earth divided among them for a reward. Calvin refers the whole to the acquiring of new territories and the accumulation of treasure, and to the distribution of conquered lands among allies: an island given up to one people, a kingdom wrested from another, borders enlarged for a third, and the spoils of a defeated tyrant handed to those who had taken care to gratify the conquerors.
40:
At the time of the end the schemes part company altogether. Keil and Delitzsch report that most modern interpreters, holding the whole second half of the chapter to concern one king, find here a last expedition against the south, and quote the ancient summary of that view before rejecting it. Ellicott says the portrait that had been fading now retains not a line: no such invasion is mentioned in history, and from the point where the western envoys turned him back he appears to have abstained from approaching them; the histories say instead that on hearing of reverses he went east on a plundering expedition, and that news of a defeat so appalled him that he fell sick for grief and died. Ellicott takes the time of the end as the end of the world, with which the end of this king coincides, and infers from the verb that the southern king begins the last conflict, in the course of which both come to an end.

Clarke and Gill each supply a later pair of powers. Clarke reasons that since the kingdoms which gave the titles no longer existed at the time meant, other northern and southern powers must be sought, and finds them in the Arabians who came from the south under their prophet and stripped a Greek emperor of his finest provinces, and in the people from the north who seized the remains of that empire, coming like a whirlwind with cavalry and many ships and taking at last the imperial city. Gill reads the same northern power throughout, and says it entered the glorious land and retains it still, notwithstanding all the attempts of European princes to get it out of his hand. Calvin refers the whole to the Romans, naming the proconsul who went south to restore a king, the danger a later general ran there after his victory in the civil war, and the fleet a rival raised with the help of a queen, after whose failure the country was reduced to a province.

The three peoples who escape are the puzzle of the passage. Keil and Delitzsch report the old explanation, that they lay out of the line of march, and agree with the critic who calls it altogether superficial, since the king would not have omitted to make war on them, as his father had done, unless they had given other proofs of their disposition. Wesley says outright that he will not hurt them because they helped him against the people of God. Ellicott finds it remarkable that these should escape while other nations fell, notes that two of them appear elsewhere as figures of the antichrist, and observes that they are called nations though after the exile they had ceased to have any distinct national existence. Clarke says they were never subdued, still occupy the deserts, and receive a yearly pension to let the pilgrim caravans pass.

Egypt is named as the great exception that fails. Keil and Delitzsch say the countries here are the same as those already overflowed, and that the southern kingdom is singled out as the most powerful, having hitherto withstood the assaults of the north and now overthrown, representing as it does the mightiest kingdoms of the earth. Ellicott says the king has at last attained his object, having been only partly successful before. Clarke applies it to a later conquest and the immense sums drawn from the country since. Calvin explains why the angel prophesies of an empire at all: he was not sent to explain the history of the whole world, but to retain the faithful in their allegiance and to persuade them to remain under the protection of God amid the most harassing convulsions, since it would be a dreadful temptation, able to overthrow all feelings of piety, that a land under divine protection should lie so exposed to robbery on every side.
43:
The treasures and the allies are quickly told. Keil and Delitzsch say that along with the countries all their treasures fall to the conqueror and the allies of the fallen kingdom must submit, taking the two peoples named as camp-followers rather than mercenaries, and as representing the most southern nations of the earth. Gill applies it to a later conquest, when many families and the treasure of a sultan were carried off to the capital. Calvin refers it to the Romans, whose avarice he calls perfectly astonishing, and says all lands should be laid open to them, so that though the cities were fortified and resisted with closed gates, none should hinder them from bursting over the whole east.

The tidings from east and north are where every voice admits ignorance or reaches for its own scheme. Gill says plainly that this and the following verse respect times yet to come and that the interpretation is not so certain, then offers two conjectures of his own. Clarke says the part is allowed to be yet unfulfilled and that the course of prophetic events will show what is portended; he gives one reading for the earlier king, whose eastern provinces were preparing to rise against him, and another for the later power he has been following. Ellicott lists three reasons why it cannot be the earlier king: he was in the east when news of his general defeat reached him, the holy land is in no sense east or north of where he then was, and he died there, not near the city. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the statements about his end contradict the historical facts, and take the tidings as reports of revolt reaching him in the south.

The tents are described with care. Gill takes the word for the tents of the princes and generals set about his own, and notes renderings that make them the tents of his cavalry, or tents covered with curtains such as distinguished the tents of kings. Keil and Delitzsch explain the unusual verb by the great palace-like tent of an oriental ruler, whose poles must be struck very deep into the earth and which was ringed by smaller tents for guards and servants, so accounting for the plural. Ellicott says the king is represented as halting while a palatial tent is erected for him, and notes that the word for palace is omitted by the Greek version and transliterated by two others as though it were a proper name. Calvin makes the tents his point: the word palace is set against frequent migrations, so that they do not measure their camp by the usage of warfare but occupy a fixed station; yet tents are named because the region was not the seat of their empire, and they attributed no more dignity to any place than was expedient for themselves.

Where the seas and the mountain are is the last question. Ellicott takes the seas as the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea, and renders the mountain literally as the mountain of the holy ornament, generally explained of Mount Zion. Keil and Delitzsch take the preposition of a space between two objects, and identify the holy hill of the delight with the mountain on which the temple stood. Calvin reports that some think the Dead Sea and the lake of asphalt intended, but himself does not hesitate for another. On the end the voices agree: Clarke says he shall make a last stand and there be smitten, all his confederate and tributary states deserting him; Wesley says God shall cut him off in the midst of his days, and when he destroys, who can help. Clarke closes by admitting that from a point near the middle the mode of interpretation is not so satisfactory, though he calls the whole a wonderful piece of prophecy and of great utility to the cause of divine revelation.
